title: Peroneal Tendon Pain in Sarasota, FL | MD Fit
description: Pain behind the outer ankle bone that lingers long after a sprain healed? Dr. Jared Caban explains peroneal tendon problems and how MD Fit rebuilds them.
lead: The peroneal tendons curve around the back of the outer ankle bone and are the main reason your ankle does not roll outward on uneven ground. They are the most commonly missed source of lingering pain after an ankle sprain that supposedly healed.

sections.h2: What peroneal tendon pain feels like
sections.html:
The pain sits at the outer ankle, specifically behind and below the bony knob, and often runs forward along the outside of the foot. Unlike a fresh sprain, it is not a single moment of injury; it builds.

  • An ache or burn behind the outer ankle bone that worsens with walking, running or standing on uneven ground.
  • Pain on pushing off, or when the foot turns inward on a kerb or in sand.
  • Occasional swelling that follows the line of the tendons rather than sitting in one lump.
  • A feeling of instability, or an ankle that keeps turning over.
  • Sometimes a snapping or clicking sensation behind the ankle bone as the tendons move.

Pressing along the tendons behind the bone reproduces it, and so does resisting the foot turning outward against your hand. Running on a cambered road, where one foot is always on the slope, is a classic trigger.

This is the important part. Most peroneal tendon problems start life as an ankle sprain that was never fully rehabilitated. The ligaments heal, the swelling goes, and everyone assumes it is done, but the peroneals have been stretched and are no longer reacting fast enough to stop the ankle rolling.

That leaves two overlapping problems, and telling them apart changes the treatment:

  • Peroneal tendinopathy is pain in the tendon itself, tender to press, sore with resisted outward movement. It is a load problem.
  • Chronic ankle instability is an ankle that gives way. It may not be especially tender. It is a control and strength problem.

They very often occur together, because a tendon working overtime to compensate for a loose ligament eventually becomes irritated. Dr. Jared tests for both rather than assuming one.

• Peroneus longus and brevis are the tendons in question. Peroneus longus runs underneath the foot to the inner arch and also helps press the big toe down; brevis attaches to the outer midfoot. Trigger points in the muscle bellies refer pain down the outer calf to the ankle, which can be mistaken for the tendon itself.
  • Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior are the opposing pull. When they dominate, the foot sits turned inward and the peroneals are on constant stretch.
  • Gastrocnemius and soleus: a tight calf limits ankle motion and pushes the foot toward the outer border on push-off.
  • Gluteus medius belongs on this list even though it is at the hip. Poor control at the hip lets the whole leg rotate inward, which puts the ankle in the position that stresses these tendons on every step.

Assess. Dr. Jared tests resisted outward foot movement, palpates the tendons behind and below the bone, checks ankle stability, calf length, balance on one leg and hip control, and looks at your shoes for wear on the outer edge. Release. Soft-tissue work along the outer calf and the peroneal muscle bellies, plus the calf complex, usually eases the pull on the tendons immediately. Correct. Balance and foot position come first, because a foot that keeps rolling will keep irritating the tendon no matter how much you strengthen it. Homework. Daily balance and controlled resisted movements from the free MD Fit app, kept short and frequent. Strengthen. Resisted outward movement progressing to heel raises with the weight guided to the outer border, then hopping, direction changes and return to court or trail.

Hip strength is built in from early on. It is routinely the missing piece in ankles that keep turning over.

1. Stop running on cambered roads and sloping beaches while this settles. Flat, even ground only.
  2. Check your shoes. Worn-down outer heels tip the foot into exactly the position that loads these tendons.
  3. Practise single-leg balance twice a day: thirty seconds on the painful side, near a wall, progressing to eyes closed when steady.
  4. Pause lateral sports such as pickleball and tennis until pushing off sideways is pain free.

sections.h2: When outer ankle pain is something else
sections.html: A fresh sprain with immediate swelling and bruising is a ligament injury and follows a different path. Pinpoint pain on the bone after a twist, especially with difficulty bearing weight, may be a fracture and needs imaging. Pain further forward on the outside of the foot at the base of the fifth metatarsal is a different bone problem entirely. Pain radiating from the outer calf without local tenderness may be referred from the peroneal muscles or from the lower back. Numbness over the top of the foot suggests nerve involvement.

Pickleball and tennis are hard on these tendons: the sideways push-off and sudden stop is exactly their job. Beach walking on a sloped shoreline loads one ankle outward with every step. And a great many people here are walking around on an ankle they sprained years ago that never got past the swelling stage. Rebuilding the peroneals and the hip together is usually what finally settles it.

timeline: Pain often eases within a few weeks once loading is controlled and balance work begins. Rebuilding enough tendon capacity and ankle control for cutting sports such as pickleball and tennis generally takes longer, and Dr. Jared progresses it on how the ankle responds rather than to a fixed schedule.
redFlags: Inability to bear weight after a twist, or pinpoint tenderness over bone: possible fracture, seek imaging.
A snap or pop behind the outer ankle with sudden weakness turning the foot outward.
A hot, red, swollen ankle with fever or feeling generally unwell.
Numbness, tingling or a cold, pale foot.
An ankle that gives way repeatedly and causes falls.

faq.q: I sprained this ankle a year ago. Could it still be the cause?
faq.a: Very often, yes. Ligaments heal but the peroneal tendons and the balance reactions around the ankle frequently do not recover on their own, and that leaves the tendon working overtime for months or years afterwards.

faq.q: What is the snapping behind my ankle?
faq.a: It can be the tendons moving over the bone. Occasionally the structure that holds them in place has been damaged and they slip forward over the bone, which a physician should assess.
A brace can help you keep playing while the tendon settles, but it does not rebuild the strength and reactions that stop the ankle rolling. Dr. Jared uses it as a bridge rather than a destination.

faq.q: Why work on my hip for an ankle problem?
faq.a: When the hip does not control the leg, the whole limb rotates inward and the foot lands in the position that stresses these tendons. Hip strength is one of the more reliable ways to stop the problem returning.
